## Q1 | Smoked Toffee

Hogsmeade has seen a recent proliferation of candy shops selling smoked toffees. The proliferation of smoked toffee makers meant the town saw a subsequent rise in *smoke*. Wood smoke can cause lung issues. Public health officials have estimated the externality to be equal to carry a cost of 6 Coins to the health of Hogsmeade residents.

::: solution

**a)** Yes. Total Surplus to buyer and seller: $5$ Coins. Marginal Social Cost: $61$ Coins. Total Surplus, including residents: $-1$ Coin. Deadweight Loss: $1$ Coin.

**b)** Yes. Total Surplus to buyer and seller: $40$ Coins. Marginal Social Cost: $46$ Coins. Total Surplus, including residents: $34$ Coins. Deadweight Loss: $0$.

**a)** The buyer’s value of $60$ is above the seller’s cost of $55$, so there is surplus to split, $60 - 55 = 5$, and the trade happens. The smoke lands on the residents, who are not part of the deal, so the buyer and seller have no reason to count it. Counting it, the toffee costs society $55 + 6 = 61$, more than the $60$ it is worth: total surplus including residents is $60 - 61 = -1$. Privately the trade looks good; socially it should not happen, and the $1$ it destroys is the deadweight loss of this exchange.

**b)** $80 > 40$, so the trade happens, with $80 - 40 = 40$ of surplus for the buyer and seller. With the smoke, the toffee costs society $40 + 6 = 46$, still well below its value of $80$, so total surplus including residents is $34$. This toffee is worth its full cost: making it creates surplus, so its deadweight loss is $0$. Banning toffee outright would throw this $34$ away. The goal is not zero toffee, only the toffees worth their full cost.

:::

### c) Market Equilibrium

Use a graph and algebra to find equilibrium price, quantity, and DWL. The demand curve and supply curve for smoked toffee can be represented using the following relationships.

$$
D: P = 20 - \frac{1}{2} Q_d \qquad\qquad S: P = 2 + Q_s
$$

:::

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::::

::: solution

Equilibrium Price $\hat{P}$: $14$ Coins. Equilibrium Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $12$ toffees. Efficient Quantity $Q^*$: $8$ toffees. Deadweight Loss: $12$ Coins.

![Smoked toffee market with the smoke cost](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every toffee adds $6$ Coins of smoke on top of the seller’s cost, so marginal social cost is supply shifted up by $6$:

$$
MSC: P = (2 + Q) + 6 = 8 + Q
$$

The market only sees the buyers’ and sellers’ curves, so it settles where demand meets supply:

$$
20 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 2 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 12, \quad P = 14
$$

The efficient quantity counts the smoke, so it sits where demand meets marginal social cost:

$$
20 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 8 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 8, \quad P = 16
$$

The market makes $4$ toffees too many. Each of the $9$th through $12$th toffees is worth more to its buyer than it costs its seller, so it trades, but it is worth less than it costs society once the smoke is counted. The $12$th, for example, is worth $14$ and costs society $8 + 12 = 20$. The losses on those toffees add up to the triangle between marginal social cost and demand from $8$ to $12$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (20 - 14) \times (12 - 8) = 12
$$

:::

## Q2 | Yard Flowers

As a small residential town, Hogsmeade has many shops and many homes near the town center. Residential homeowners often plant flowers in their front yards, contributing to the positive atmosphere in town. There are numerous garden stores selling supplies for planting and growing many varieties. The supply and demand relationships for a dozen flowers is given by the following equations, with prices in Coins.

$$
D: P = 100 - \frac{1}{2} Q_d \qquad\qquad S: P = \frac{1}{2} Q_s
$$

Recently, a study found a positive impact on the wellbeing of the community from the flowers planted in the front yards of their neighbors. The impact was estimated to carry a value of 10 Coins per dozen flowers planted. Use a graph and algebra to calculate the size of the market failure by identifying and calculating the deadweight loss.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Equilibrium Quantity ($\hat{Q}$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

Efficient Quantity ($Q^*$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::::

:::: {.columns .continued gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Deadweight Loss (*DWL*):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

:::

::::

::: solution

Equilibrium Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $100$ dozen. Efficient Quantity $Q^*$: $110$ dozen. Deadweight Loss: $50$ Coins.

![Yard flower market with the neighbors’ benefit](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Demand is each homeowner’s own value of a dozen flowers, the marginal private benefit. The neighbors enjoy another $10$ per dozen, so marginal social benefit is demand shifted up by $10$:

$$
MSB: P = \left(100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q\right) + 10 = 110 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q
$$

The market settles where demand meets supply:

$$
100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 100, \quad P = 50
$$

The efficient quantity counts the neighbors’ benefit, so it sits where marginal social benefit meets supply:

$$
110 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 110, \quad P = 55
$$

The market plants $10$ dozen too few. A homeowner deciding on one more dozen weighs only their own enjoyment against the price; the neighbors’ $10$ never enters the decision. So the dozens from $100$ to $110$, which cost more than the homeowner values them but less than they are worth to the whole town, go unplanted. The surplus they would have created is the triangle between marginal social benefit and supply from $100$ to $110$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (55 - 45) \times (110 - 100) = 50
$$

:::
